title: Audio Lesson: Hooks and Extensions
limitations: Generated from concept pages; not yet reviewed.
Content may drift from source; verify against current main.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In this lesson, we explore hooks and extensions — the mechanism that lets users attach custom logic to every agent lifecycle event. Think of it like middleware for your agent's event stream.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The HookRegistry wraps any EventSink. When the runtime emits an event — say, a tool call request — before-hooks fire first. They can continue, block, or modify the event data. After the inner sink processes it, after-hooks run for audit purposes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Five built-in hook patterns cover common needs: protected paths block access to sensitive files like dot-env. Protected commands block dangerous shell operations like rm-rf. Stop verification prevents the agent from claiming victory without evidence. Output sanitization redacts API keys from tool output. And external signal injection lets CI pipelines or webhooks push data into agent context.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The trust boundary is all-or-nothing. In untrusted workspaces, every hook is disabled — registration raises an error, and events pass straight through. This prevents malicious workspace code from intercepting agent operations.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Error isolation is critical. A hook that raises an exception or times out never crashes the pipeline. The exception is caught, logged, and the event continues normally. This makes hooks safe to experiment with.
